extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in evolutionary biology, biometry, and quantitative studies of selection
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for quantitatively detecting and characterizing natural and sexual selection in populations — what to measure, how to distinguish periodic vs secular change, and which mating systems promote differentiation. Emphasis on statistical/observational methods across generations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting selection via change in statistical constants
rubrics_metrics.description: To test whether selection is taking place or not we must test whether one or more of these constants vary between one adult generation and a second.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare numerical descriptors of a character (type/mode, mean, standard deviation, coefficients of correlation) measured for the same race at the same growth stage across two generations. Changes in type or variability between epochs indicate selection. This comparison separates effects of growth and death and helps distinguish periodic from secular selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of skewness
rubrics_metrics.description: Such distributions are termed skew. It is found convenient to measure this skewness by the ratio of the distance between mode and mean to the standard deviation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute skewness as (mean - mode)/standard_deviation (or distance between mode and mean divided by SD) to quantify asymmetry and track sign/changes of skewness between epochs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining selective versus non-selective death-rates by polygon reduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce the frequency polygon of the post-selection epoch until it just falls inside (touches) the pre-selection polygon; the point of contact corresponds to the organ value for which the death-rate is non-selective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Graphical procedure: scale down the second-epoch polygon (representing survivors as a fraction of original) until it just lies within the original polygon; where they touch there is no selective intercept and the selective death-rate vanishes. From this construction one can obtain numerical constants describing relative death-rates and determine the organ value 'best fitted to survive'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining relative selective death-rates among organ values
rubrics_metrics.description: We are able, however, to determine the relative selective death-rate for organs of different sizes; thus the selective death-rate of an organ of value 5 is to that of one of value 11 as df5 is to df11.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if absolute rates aren't known, the relative selective death-rate across character values can be derived from the graphical/analytic comparisons of frequency polygons and their reductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements to obtain absolute proportion of selective vs non-selective death-rates
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to determine the proportion of the selective and non-selective death-rates we must ascertain the value of n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value of n (overall mortality factor) can only be obtained by (i) following the same individuals during the selection period (possible in man or captive organisms), or (ii) measuring the total actual reduction of adult life in some limited area during the epoch assuming no migration. Both methods have practical limitations (migration, growth/influx).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare same stage across generations to distinguish periodic vs secular selection
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine whether selection is periodic or secular, we must measure our organ or character for the same race in two generations at the same stage of growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Periodic selection may merely maintain a race (recurrent each generation) whereas secular selection produces progressive change; only by matching growth stage across generations can one infer permanence/progression of change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishing whether secular selection can produce speciation
rubrics_metrics.description: We want to know whether the changes, if secular, are capable of differentiating one form of life into two ... relatively or absolutely infertile, i.e. are capable of giving an account of the origin of species?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantitative observation and experiment are required to test (i) whether changes are secular, (ii) whether secular changes lead to differentiation accompanied by barriers to intercrossing, and (iii) whether rates of change are sufficient to account for observed speciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of correlation between reproductive traits and selected traits for speciation
rubrics_metrics.description: We must first show that the reproductive organs or their modes of functioning are correlated with the organs selected, and that the differentiation here is so great that physiologically or mechanically mutual fertility of the two types is impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To claim differentiation into species, demonstrate quantitative correlations linking selected characters to reproductive morphology/behavior or show mechanisms (timing, habit) that reduce inter-fertility; otherwise isolation cannot produce species-level infertility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of forms of selective mating (mating-system rubric)
rubrics_metrics.description: We may ... classify the forms of selective mating in the following manner: (a) Autogamic mating (self-fertilisation); (b) Endogamic mating (within family/brood/clan); (c) Homogamic mating (mating of like with like; assortative); (d) Apolegamic mating (preferential mating; sexual selection in Darwin's narrow sense); (e) Heterogamic mating (mating of unlikes); (f) Pangamic mating (random mating).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these categories to evaluate a population's tendency toward differentiation: (a)-(e) can promote differentiation and establishment of distinct stocks under selection; (f) pangamy (random mating) tends to check differentiation. Definitions and nuances (e.g., autogamy including selfing and certain within-plant crosses) are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and definition of sexual selection (broad and narrow senses)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Darwinian theory of evolution really requires three factors: (a) Natural selection; (b) Inheritance of characters; (c) Sexual selection, leading to differential fertility. By sexual selection I would understand something rather more than Darwin includes by that term, namely, all differential mating due to taste, habit, or circumstance, which prevents a form of life from freely intercrossing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating the origin of species, treat sexual selection broadly as any preferential mating that reduces free intercrossing and, over time, can produce barriers to gene flow and differential fertility. Quantify intensity of preferential mating and its effect on mating patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measuring mating patterns and fertility correlations
rubrics_metrics.description: Does like really mate with like, and, if so, how is the intensity of this mating to be measured? Is fertility actually correlated with physical characters likely to form the material for selection? Can we trace any differentiation of mutual fertility with differentiation in type?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical criteria: measure assortative mating strength, quantify fertility in se and inter se (within and between types), and assess statistical correlations between fertility and the characters under selection; these measures are essential to test mechanisms of differentiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inheritance properties relevant to population distributions and stock establishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Just as all the progeny of an individual of organ or character a form an array with definite variability, nor is the type of this array, that is, its mean, identical with a, but with an organ whose quantitative value is nearer to the modal value c. ... We can, however, establish a breed or stock giving offspring of the same type ... if we select ... for several reproductive stages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for regression toward the mean (offspring mean nearer to population mode than parent), use mid-parent concept for bisexual reproduction, and recognize that sustained directional selection across multiple generations (not single-generation selection) is required to fix a new stock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for quantitative/statistical methods and experimental approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not absence of explanation, but rather of the quantitative testing of explanations, which hinders at this point the development of the Darwinian theory. We want numerical observation and quantitative experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply statistical analyses (frequency polygons, surfaces, multiple correlation, regression, hyperspace geometry) and designed experiments (transfers to new environments, laboratory selection) to quantify selection, differentiation, and rates of change; beware confounding factors like migration and growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying the organ value 'fittest to survive'
rubrics_metrics.description: We can also determine the organ fittest to survive, i.e. the organ for which the selective death-rate vanishes; it will not necessarily coincide with the modal value before or after selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From graphical/analytic construction of pre- and post-selection distributions, identify the character value at which selective mortality is non-differential. Do not assume this equals the mode.
